activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
Eleanor stood in the middle of Grandma Rosa's living room with a folded paper in her hand, and the paper might as well have been written in a language she didn't speak. In two weeks she would stand in front of her whole extended family at her coming-of-age ceremony and recite the blessing from memory, and so far she could only remember the first two lines. She'd read it aloud forty times in her bedroom. The words slid off her brain like water off a duck's back.

"Grandma," she said, "how did you learn it when you were twelve?"

Grandma Rosa was dusting the bookshelf, and she paused with the rag in midair. "I didn't learn it in a bedroom," she said. "I learned it right here, in this house, one line in each room. Then I'd walk through in my head and the lines would be waiting for me where I left them."

"Waiting where?"

"Where I put them." Grandma Rosa tapped the mantel. "First line, right there, next to the clock. Walk the house, girl. See what happens."

Eleanor read the first line of the blessing aloud, then set it down beside the clock the way she'd set a cup on a table. In the kitchen she placed the second line on the counter beside the bread box. The third line she laid across the bathroom mirror, and the fourth along the stairs, one step at a time. She felt a little silly, handing invisible words to furniture, but she kept going: the fifth line on her grandmother's bed, the sixth in the closet where the winter coats hung like a quiet alliance of sleeves. When she reached the back porch, she only had the last line left, so she tucked it under the watering can.

Then she went back to the living room, closed her eyes, and walked the route in her mind. Clock, counter, mirror, stairs, bed, closet, watering can. Each place held its line, and as she pictured herself moving through the house, the words arrived in order, whole and unhurried.

She opened her eyes and recited the entire blessing, start to finish, without the paper. Her voice came out steady, but her hands were shaking.

Grandma Rosa set down the dusting rag. "Say it again."

Eleanor said it again. On the second time through, she stumbled at the bathroom mirror and had to picture herself actually standing in the doorway, feeling the cold tile under her feet, before the line surfaced. The trick worked, she realized, but only if she truly saw each place. It was like diving underwater; she had to submerge herself in the room, not just glance at it. A memory half-visited was a memory vulnerable to slipping away entirely.

"So that's how you did it," Eleanor said. "You'd just walk the house."

"Every night before bed, from the time I was your age." Grandma Rosa smiled. "My mother called it the method of loci. Loci means places."

That night, in her own bedroom across town, Eleanor closed her eyes and walked the familiar route again: clock, counter, mirror, stairs, bed, closet, watering can. The words rose up to meet her, room by room, all the way to the porch. She whispered the last line into the dark, then reached for the lamp switch.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
story:
Connor had wanted the part of the narrator in the spring play, the safe person who stands at a podium with a script. Instead, Ms. Ruiz's sign-up sheet had said everyone must do improv, and now he stood on the auditorium stage under hot lights with a partner he barely knew, a girl named Priya who chewed her pencil like it owed her money.

"Any scene," Ms. Ruiz called from the third row. "Just talk. I'll watch."

Priya cupped her hands around her mouth. "Captain, the ship is leaking!"

"We're not on a ship," Connor said. "We're in math class."

The lights stayed the same, the rows of empty seats stayed the same, but something in the room changed anyway. Priya's arms dropped to her sides. Nobody laughed, and the silence had weight to it, like the whole auditorium had turned desolate in a single sentence. Ms. Ruiz made a small mark on her clipboard and did not say what it was for.

They tried again after two other pairs went. Priya opened a door that wasn't there and said, "Careful, we just installed a new security system in this museum." Connor almost said there was no museum, and then he noticed the pattern: every time someone on this stage said "no, that's not what this is," the scene died, and every time someone agreed, it grew. When Marcus had claimed a stray dog was his, his partner had said "no, that's not your dog," and the audience had gone so quiet Connor heard the radiator. Marcus had muttered afterward, "She was blocking me." That was the word. Blocking was rejecting or ignoring your partner's offer, and it stopped everything.

"Yes," Connor said now, "and the alarm is set to go off if anyone touches the giant diamond." He pointed at an empty pedestal.

Priya froze in a crouch, one hand stretched toward nothing. "The diamond is at the equator," she whispered. "In a vault. On a boat."

Connor didn't argue that vaults at the equator made no sense. "Then we sail," he said, and spun an invisible wheel.

The third row made a noise like actual laughter. Priya staggered as if the deck was rolling, and Connor grabbed an invisible rope and hauled on it, leaning back so hard he nearly fell into the curtains.

"Captain," she shouted, "the wheel is coming off in my hands!"

"Then hold the wheel," Connor said, "and I'll install a new one."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
story:
Alexandra snapped the covers off her little brother's blanket fort and yelled, "I told you to keep out of my room!" Leo stared at her, one foam sword drooping, and then he started to cry. She hadn't even noticed him come in. She'd been sitting at her desk staring at the same math problem for twenty minutes, and her fingers were gripping her pencil so hard they ached.

Afterward she sat on her bed feeling terrible, so she did what she always did when something confused her: she made a list in her notebook. She wrote down the week. Monday she'd quit her guitar practice after five minutes, which was strange because she loved the new song. Tuesday she'd snapped at her best friend Priya over a text message about nothing. Wednesday she couldn't finish her homework because she kept rereading the same paragraph. Thursday was today. She underlined the four items twice.

"There's a pattern here," she said out loud. Leo, still sniffing, peeked through the blanket she'd dismantled from his fort. "What kind of pattern?" he asked. "The kind you can't see directly," Alexandra said. "Like when the lamp doesn't turn on and you check the bulb, but the real problem is that the lamp got unplugged." Leo frowned. "I unplugged it once," he admitted. "For the fort lights."

She thought about the unplugged lamp. Something had to be causing the pattern, something underneath. Then she landed on it. The spelling bee tryouts were next Friday. She'd been picked last year and messed up on the word "biased" in the final round, and now that the tryouts were coming again, everything felt off. She wrote a new heading at the top of the list: not "things that went wrong" but "signs." Losing interest in guitar. Snapping at friends. Trouble concentrating. Yelling at Leo. Those weren't four separate problems. They were signs of one thing.

"Leo," she said, coming out of her room, "I'm sorry I yelled. I think I've been stressed about the spelling bee and it came out sideways at you." Leo considered this. "So you're like a soda can that got shaken up." "Exactly like that," Alexandra said. "Now I have to open it slowly." Leo wanted to help, because helping meant staying up past bedtime. "Teach me the slow opening," he demanded. "It's called deep breathing," she said. "You breathe in for four counts and out for four counts."

They sat on the hallway floor together, breathing like two sleeping dragons, which made Leo dissolve into giggles every third breath. Alexandra kept going anyway. In, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four. Her shoulders dropped away from her ears. It felt like the fizz settling back down.

That night she built a routine around it. Guitar practice right after dinner, so the song wasn't left undone. Screens off an hour before bed. The same three things in the same order every night: breathing, brushing teeth, reading one chapter of her book about family heritage, because tracing her grandmother's journey across the ocean made her mind go quiet.

On Friday she stood in line for tryouts, her heart tapping fast. She breathed in for four and out for four, and when the teacher said "biased," she spelled it without a single stumble. Afterward Priya hugged her, and Leo held up a hand-made sign that said GO ALAXANDRA, which was spelled wrong in four different places. Alexandra laughed until her sides hurt. "Close enough," she said. "You're a sign of something too, you know." "Of what?" Leo asked. "Of a good week," she said, and spun the misspelled sign around like a prize.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
The art gallery's back room smelled like pencil shavings and old paper, and Max had been there for two hours trying to draw a street that didn't look like it had been sat on. He was there because the gallery was holding a contest for young artists, and the winner's drawing would hang in the front window for a whole month. Max wanted that window more than he wanted lunch, and that was saying something, because his sandwich in his backpack was a genuinely nutritious one and he knew it.

He'd been copying a print on the wall, a painting of a guild hall on a long street, and something about it bothered him. All the lines of the buildings slanted toward a single dot far in the distance, like the whole street was being pulled into a funnel. Max had tried the same trick on his own drawing, but his street looked crooked, wrong, like it was sliding off the page. He pressed his pencil down so hard the tip snapped. "Come on," he muttered, and the old man asleep on the bench across the room opened one eye.

"You're fighting it," the old man said. He didn't say anything else. He just pointed at the print, then at the window, then went back to sleep, which Max decided was the most annoying way possible to give advice.

Max went to the window. Outside was Elm Street, running straight away from the gallery, and when he looked down it, he could see only the fronts of the buildings facing him, square and flat like the faces of playing cards, while their sides squeezed inward toward one tiny point way at the end, where the street seemed to swallow itself. Then he walked to the corner and looked down Cross Street from the side. The fronts didn't face him anymore. The lines went off in two directions, and his one dot was useless, like trying to catch rain in a fork.

He raced back to the bench, grabbed his sketchbook, and planted himself square in the middle of the window, facing dead-on down Elm Street. He drew the dot first, right in the center, and pretended it was a tiny magic mouth eating the street. Every slanted line, roofs and curbs and window ledges, he aimed straight at the dot's hungry little face, and the buildings leaned in like they were listening to a secret. He laughed out loud when the street suddenly appeared, deep and real, as if he could step into his own drawing. The sleeping man said, without opening his eyes, "Now you're not fighting it."

That night Max wrote a note and taped it to the wall above his desk: "Dear Future Max. The trick is you have to be looking straight down the street, so the fronts of things face you and everything else runs to the one dot. From the corner it doesn't work. Also, the old man on the bench might be a wizard. Investigate. Yours, Max." He read it twice, nodded, and turned off the light.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
story:
Marble races were banned in the cafeteria after the Great Ketchup Incident, so Charlotte and Priya had claimed the science lab at lunch, where the long black counters made the best tracks in the school. Priya's marble, a cloudy green one she called Gherkin, had beaten Charlotte's steel marble four times in a row.

"That's not fair," Charlotte said, watching Gherkin click into the tray of sand at the end of the counter. "You start yours higher on the ramp every single time."

"It rolled farther," Priya said, which was true, but it wasn't the whole truth, and Charlotte could feel it. A marble that rolled a longer distance in the same time was faster, sure. But a marble that rolled the same distance in less time was faster too, and nobody was timing anything. They were comparing apples to pineapples.

She pulled a meter stick and the classroom stopwatch out of the drawer, along with a chunk of chalky rock from the mineral shelf. "New rules. We measure."

Priya groaned but helped. They marked a start line and a finish line exactly one meter apart on the counter, so the distance would be the same for both marbles. Then they rolled. Gherkin crossed the meter in 2.4 seconds. Charlotte's steel marble took only 1.8 seconds, which stung, because now she was losing by actual numbers instead of just by vibes.

"Wait," Priya said slowly, chewing the end of her braid. "Yours took less time. Does that mean yours is faster?"

"Same distance, less time. Yeah." Charlotte wrote both numbers in her notebook, then frowned at them. "But what if the distances aren't the same? Like on the ramp, where you start high?"

They tried it. Priya rolled Gherkin down the ramp and let it travel 1.5 meters before it stopped, and it took 3 seconds. Charlotte divided the distance by the time on scrap paper, tongue between her teeth. 1.5 divided by 3 gave 0.5. Her steel marble on the same ramp went 1.2 meters in 2 seconds, which gave 0.6. The numbers were in meters per second now, and even though Gherkin had rolled farther, the steel marble had the bigger number, so the steel marble was faster. Average speed equals distance divided by time. It was like the marble had left a signature behind, a number you could read even after it stopped moving.

"We can graph it," Charlotte said. On graph paper she put time along the bottom and distance up the side, and the two lines climbed like hiking trails. The steeper line was the faster marble, so you could see the speed, actually see it, in the slant.

They got so absorbed that Priya knocked the beaker of water set out for fourth period, and Gherkin rolled off the table straight into the spill. Charlotte fished it out before the paper towels could submerge it completely. "Your marble is not porous, thankfully," she said, drying it on her sleeve. "If it were, it would soak up the whole spill."

"It's glass, Charlotte. It's the least porous thing in this room besides you at lunch."

Charlotte laughed so hard the graph lines wobbled. She pinned the finished chart to the corkboard and stepped back. "Okay. Same ramp, same meter, stopwatch. Best of three. And Gherkin gets the outside lane, because the counter has a bump out there."

Priya grinned and set her marble on the line. "Ready, set, physics."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
story:
Sofia counted the bills in her canvas pouch twice, and both times the answer was the same: forty-one dollars. The pottery bowl she wanted at the third row of stalls cost sixty, and the potter had told her she was holding it for one more Saturday only. Sofia had sold three jars of her grandmother's peach jam that morning, and she had two more Saturdays' worth of selling ahead of her, but the numbers refused to add up.

Her friend Marcus sat beside her behind the jam table, fanning himself with a paper bag. "You could just put the money in the bank," he said. "My sister's account earns interest."

"That takes forever," Sofia said, though the word interest snagged in her mind. In math class last week they had plotted two savings accounts on the same grid, and something about those lines had bothered her ever since. She grabbed the brown paper bag from Marcus, smoothed it flat, and borrowed his pencil.

"Five years," she muttered, drawing the axes. "Fifty dollars, five percent." She plotted the first account year by year, marking a dot for each balance and connecting them. The line climbed steadily, the same amount of climb every single year. Then she started the second account, the one their teacher had labeled compound, and here the dots drifted apart from the first set. The gap between the two lines started out as a sliver, so thin she almost missed it, but by the fourth year it was obvious, and by the fifth year the second line had pulled clearly above the first. It didn't just climb. It bent upward, rising more in the later years than in the early ones.

"Look," she said, holding up the bag. "See how mine's a straight line and this one curves?" Marcus leaned in, squinting past a woman buying a jar of apricot preserves. "The compound one," Sofia said, tapping the curve, "gains more each year than the year before."

"That's the one you want," Marcus said. "Obviously."

She almost agreed with him. Then she stopped, pencil hovering. Five years was a long time. She would be eighteen. The potter's bowl was here now, and no amount of curved lines would produce it by Saturday. "Compound is better in the long run," she said slowly, "but simple still grows. My line didn't stay flat either."

"So what do you do?" Marcus asked.

Sofia folded the bag and tucked it into her pouch next to the forty-one dollars. She would open an account Monday, with every dollar she didn't need for the bowl, and she would keep plotting both lines each month just to watch the gap widen with her own eyes. For now, though, there were two Saturdays of jam to sell. She stood, lifted the last jar into the sunlight where its amber color caught a customer's eye, and called out, "Peach jam, three dollars, and I'll tell you why you should bank the change!"

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
story:
Kate stood under the dome of the planetarium with her poster board balanced against a chair, and for the hundredth time she checked the drawing of Earth on its tilted axis. Tomorrow she had to explain the seasons to her class, and Mrs. Okafor had offered the planetarium after school as a place to practice. The dome glowed with a slow wheel of stars, and beside her, Dex fiddled with the projector controls, because what Dex wanted, more than anything, was to be promoted from "poster holder" to "special effects operator."

"Watch this," Dex said, and stabbed a button. The dome went black, then blazed with a spinning hurricane of green dots. "That's not seasons," Kate said. "That's a screen saver." Dex adjusted knobs until a huge orange sun hung over a slowly turning Earth, and Kate pointed at the tilted line she had drawn through it. "Okay, run it to June. When the north pole tips toward the sun, that's our summer, and the longest day of the whole year."

She had rehearsed the ending a dozen times: longest day, hottest day, done, bow. But when she flipped to her temperature chart taped beside the poster, she stopped. The highest bar on the chart, the record scorcher from the news last summer, sat in late July, weeks after the longest day. "That can't be right," she muttered, tracing the bars with her finger. If the longest day wasn't the hottest, then something about her whole explanation was off, and tomorrow she would stand up there and say something wrong.

Dex leaned over her shoulder, chewing a pretzel. "Maybe your chart is hypothetical," he offered. "You know. Made up." "It's not made up, it's from the weather station," Kate said, but a small despair crept in anyway. Then she looked at the dome again, at the fat orange sun hanging over the turning Earth, and a new idea rose in her. A chart couldn't lie twice. She could infer from the pattern itself: every summer, the hottest weeks landed several weeks after the longest day, which meant the day length and the heat didn't peak together. Something took time. She grabbed her marker and wrote it in big letters across the bottom of the poster: land and oceans take time to warm up.

"The longest day and the hottest day aren't the same day," she said slowly, testing it aloud. "The heat shows up later. Like the Earth is a giant pot of water that doesn't boil the second you light the stove." Dex stopped chewing. "Wait. So summer is actually a delayed reaction?" "Basically," Kate said, and laughed at how obvious it now seemed, hiding in plain sight in her own chart.

"Can I put that in the show?" Dex asked, hovering over the controls. "Like, the sun comes on full blast, and then the dome turns red slowly, later, for the heat?" Kate thought of tomorrow, of twenty classmates staring up at a dome glowing red on a delay, and nodded. "Do it," she said. Dex slid the fader up, and the whole sky began, gradually, to burn.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
story:
Alexis set the duet sheet on the piano rack and nodded at Priya, who stood ready with her flute. The piece was called "Autumn Walk," and Mr. Delgado had said they'd perform it Friday if it was ready. The top of the first page said Andante in curly letters, and Alexis was sure that meant fast, because it looked like the word "gallop." He plunged in at top speed, fingers flying, and within four measures the whole thing collapsed. Priya's line tangled into his, they stopped, and she stared at him like he'd stepped on her foot.

"Where did that come from?" she asked. "You practiced it slow yesterday."

He had, and that gave him a clue. Alexis tried to diagnose the problem like his older sister Mara taught him last summer, when her caterpillar stopped moving. "Don't guess," she had said, turning the jar toward the light. "Observe, then change one thing." The larva had been still for two days, and Mara refused to panic; she'd simply waited, kept the jar warm, and eventually a butterfly pushed out. Alexis had learned that a creature could look finished and still be in the middle of changing. Maybe his piece was like that too.

He changed one thing: the speed. He played the same notes at the slow, easy pace he'd used the day before, and Priya slid in beside him, her flute line fitting over his like a lid on a box. It worked, but it didn't make sense. Why would fast fail and slow work, on a page that said Andante? Then he remembered the poster on the music room wall, the one with Italian words nobody ever read. He crossed the room and found the row of tempo words. "Largo means very slow," he read aloud, running his finger along. "Andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively."

"Andante is walking," Priya said, catching up. "So the title, Autumn Walk, it's a clue. The whole first page is supposed to stroll."

They played it again, and Alexis felt the piece click into place, strolling, then lifting when the page turned to Allegro, bright and quick. The difference was significant; it wasn't the same song at all when the speed matched the words. They ran it twice more, and the second time Priya added a little swell on the loud parts, and Alexis matched her without being asked.

At the door, Priya paused. "One problem. Friday, Mr. Delgado is making us swap parts. I take the piano, you take the flute."

Alexis looked at the flute case, then at her grin, and picked it up. "Then I'd better start walking," he said.

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
story:
The erosion table at the Riverworks exhibit had a line of kids behind it, and Payton intended to be at the front of that line before the museum's demo hour started at two o'clock. The trick was that Ms. Ferrante, the docent, only picked one visitor to run the canyon model, and she always picked someone who could explain what they were doing. Payton had been at the table for twenty minutes, watching a trickle of water slice through a slope of gray sand, and she had a theory.

"Move over," said her little brother, Dex. He wanted one thing at the museum, which was to jam both hands into the water channel and see what happened. That was his whole agenda. "You're not even doing anything. You're just staring."

"I'm staring scientifically." Payton pointed at the bend where the water slowed. "See how the sand piles up on the inside of the curve? That's deposition. The water drops the stuff it carried." She traced the cut bank on the outside of the bend, where the sand had been eaten away into a steep little cliff. "And that's erosion. Take away there, dump it here. If you did that for a really long time, you'd get something huge."

"Like what?"

Payton turned to the photo panel behind the table, a wide shot of the Grand Canyon with its stair-stepped walls. Below it, a brass plaque said that scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago. She read it twice. Six million years of take-away-there, dump-it-here. She looked at the tabletop canyon she'd made in forty minutes, which was about the size of a loaf of bread, and decided not to do the math.

"Ms. Ferrante," she called. "Can I try the plateau model?"

Ms. Ferrante raised an eyebrow. "Tell me why the water cuts down instead of just spreading out, and it's yours. Others tried already. I exclude anyone who guesses."

"Because the plateau is raised up, so the water has somewhere to go down," Payton said. "The river stays in one channel and keeps sawing at the same spot, and everything it saws off gets deposited downstream. It's the most probable way a canyon gets deep instead of just wide."

Ms. Ferrante stepped aside. "Go."

Payton opened the valve. The water dropped off the plateau edge and began chewing through the sand, quick and businesslike, exactly like her theory said it would. Dex crept closer with both hands out.

"One finger," Payton said, holding the valve. "That's my final offer."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
On the second Wednesday of camp, Leah sat on the dock with her knees pulled up, watching the paddleboards revolve slowly around the buoy like ducks who had lost their map. Her cabinmate Priya sat three feet away, eating dry cereal out of a bag and pretending not to hear the boys behind them.

"Nice goggles, Priya," Marco called for the third time that day. "Did your grandma pick those out? Oh wait, your grandma can't see either."

His friend Dylan laughed like the joke had just gotten funnier, which it had not, since it had been the same joke since Monday. Priya put the cereal away and stared at the water.

Leah wanted to say something, but last summer she had tried "Leave her alone" at a different camp, and the teasing had simply turned around and landed on her, then doubled back onto the girl she'd tried to help, like a wasp that gets angrier when you swat. She chewed on the problem. The teasing happened when counselors weren't close. It happened at the dock, at the canteen, on the trail. That was a pattern, and patterns had rules, and rules could maybe be used.

"You should tell Becca," Leah said quietly.

Priya shook her head fast. "Then I'm a snitch. It'll just get worse."

"Telling a trusted adult is not tattling," Leah said, "when the goal is to protect someone from harm rather than to get someone in trouble." She had read that somewhere, maybe in the camp handbook, maybe in the memoir her mom kept in the bathroom, the one about the lady who rescued sea turtles. Either way, she was pretty sure it was a real rule and not just a nice idea.

"So what's the difference?" Priya asked. "Becca punishes Marco, he hates me more."

"Then we don't make it about punishment." Leah stood up and brushed pine needles off her shorts. "We make it about where they can't do it anymore."

They found Becca by the craft shed, gluing googly eyes onto a wooden owl with an expression that can only be described as obstinate. Leah explained the pattern: dock, canteen, trail, whenever no adult was near. Becca listened, then said she'd rearrange the buddy groups and put a junior counselor on the dock rotation, and she would not say who had mentioned anything.

The next afternoon, a junior counselor appeared on the dock with a whistle and a book about lighthouses. Marco got through exactly one "Nice goggles" before he realized he was performing for an audience of one adult and zero laughs. He went quiet. Dylan drifted off to bother a paddleboard.

"They didn't get in trouble at all," Priya said, sounding almost disappointed.

"I know," Leah said. "Weird how protecting you didn't require ruining them."

Priya held out the bag of dry cereal. Leah took a handful, and they watched the paddleboards keep circling the buoy, going nowhere, stubborn as ever.

"Grandma did pick the goggles," Priya admitted. "They're mirrored. She said they make me look like a spy."

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
story:
Laurence set her easel on the flattest patch of grass behind the garage, where the morning sun wouldn't move the shadows too fast. She was painting her little brother, Theo, who sat on an overturned bucket holding still about as well as a kettle before it boils. Her art book lay open on the grass to a page she had read three times the night before. Glazing, the book said, means brushing a thin transparent wash over a layer that is completely dry, so the colours mix optically instead of blending together on the paper. She wanted that glow the book promised, cheeks that looked warm from underneath, not painted on top like a stereotype of a doll with two pink circles stamped on its face.

She laid down the first wash, pale peach over the whole face, and it went beautifully. Then came the hard part. Shadows. The book said to build them in layers, light to dark, each one dry before the next. But Theo kept squirming, and the light was climbing the fence, and Laurence had once spent a whole rainy afternoon waiting for paint to dry and had sworn never to waste an afternoon like that again.

"Just the cheek," she told herself, dipping her brush. "One little shadow. It's practically dry."

It wasn't practically dry. The moment her grey-violet wash touched the peach, the two colours ran together and bloomed into a cloudy brown blotch, right on Theo's cheekbone. Laurence winced. Theo leaned over to look.

"You gave me a bruise," he said.

"It's mud," she said. "Go back to being a bucket-sitter."

She stared at the blotch. The paper was still shiny where the peach layer hadn't finished drying, and she realized the wet grey had sunk into it instead of sitting on top. Last night's waiting hadn't been wasted time at all. It had been the whole point.

"I'm testing something," she announced. She painted a small stripe of the same grey on a corner of the paper where the first wash had dried completely, then waited, checking it every minute. Grandpa's office smelled like pencil shavings and old coffee, which was strange because Christopher had never once seen Grandpa sharpen a pencil. He had recruited Grandpa as his official number tester, and Grandpa took the job seriously, sitting beside him with a glass of lemonade he called "the good nectar, straight from the plastic jug."

"Type in a seven," Grandpa said. "Seven is prime. I'd bet the ranch on it, if I had a ranch."

Christopher ran the program. IS 7 PRIME? the screen asked, in the polite way he had coded it. He typed 7 and pressed Enter. NO, said the program.

Grandpa raised an eyebrow. "Either seven has changed its ways, or your machine is handing us a counterfeit answer."

Christopher slumped back in the chair. It got worse. He tried 2, 3, 11, even 13, his own favorite. Every single one came back NO. "Every number can't be not prime," he muttered. "That's like saying every coin in the world is counterfeit." Grandpa toasted him with the nectar and said nothing, which was Grandpa for figure it out yourself, kid.

Christopher scrolled up to the loop. He had written a line that marched through possible divisors, and he stared at it until his eyes felt sandy. Then he leaned in. The loop, he realized, was going too far. In Python, range(2, n) produced the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1, so it tried every possible divisor except 1 and n itself. His loop didn't stop there. It kept going and included n itself, so it divided n by n, and n always went into n with nothing left over, and the program declared everything not prime.

"So seven wasn't lying," Christopher said out loud. "I was making it divide seven by seven." Grandpa snorted lemonade halfway down his chin.

Christopher deleted the extra letter in the range, the way you'd flick a bug off a picnic blanket, and ran it again. He typed 7. YES, said the program, with what Christopher swore was a smug little font. He typed 15. NO. He typed 13. YES, and he pointed at the screen with both index fingers like a game show contestant.

Grandpa set down his glass and cracked his knuckles. "All right, hotshot. Feed it a big one. Give it 91."

Christopher's fingers hovered over the keys. "You're just trying to stump it."

"I am absolutely trying to stump it," Grandpa said. "Type."

"I didn't know you'd be here," Ellie said. Devorah's grandfather had died in the spring, and her family had sat shiva for a week. Ellie had gone over twice with a plate of her mother's coffee cake.

"We come every Sunday before it gets hot," Devorah said. She was holding a small stone in her fist, turning it over and over. "He said you won't actually find that phrase in the Hebrew Bible. People say it anyway. My grandma says it every time she lights a candle."

Ellie turned that over. At church, her pastor read about heaven straight from the page and pointed to the verse, and her mother could find it in under a minute with the ribbon bookmarks in her Bible. Devorah's family had a phrase that everyone used, and it came from somewhere else, from people talking to each other over a long time, the way a path gets worn across grass even though nobody paved it. The two ideas were not the same, and they were not opposite either. They were just two different maps for a place nobody had come back from, which was something Ellie could not check no matter how she tested it. She could not convey the whole shape of the thought to Devorah in words, so she said only, "My mom looks everything up. She'd drive your cousin crazy."

"Devorah taught me," Ellie said. "We're going to walk home together."

story:
Owen spread his pencil, ruler, and eraser across the kitchen table and stared at the blank page like it owed him money. His art teacher had said their street drawings were due Monday, and Owen had picked one-point perspective because it sounded impressive. Now he had to figure out what it actually was. He drew a dot in the middle of the page and two diagonal lines running out from it toward the corners, then stopped. A dot and two lines did not look like a street. They looked like a tent, or a very open bird.

His older sister Nadia came in for a snack, saw the page, and slid her own drawing onto the table beside it. "We're doing the same project," she said. Hers showed a row of shops marching away toward a dot, with windows, doors, and even a striped awning on the bakery. Owen leaned closer, and then he leaned back, because something about it was wrong. The buildings in front looked like they were tipping over sideways, leaning against each other like tired people waiting for a bus.

"You slanted everything," Owen said.

"You have to," Nadia said. "That's the whole trick. All the lines go to the vanishing point."

Owen looked from her drawing to his own dot. "But those shops are facing us. Straight on." He picked up her pencil and held it upright against the shop window in the front of her drawing. "See? When I hold it this way, your window top goes down at an angle. But look out the actual window at Mrs. Petty's house across the street." They both turned and looked. The upstairs windows, straight ahead of them, ran flat and level, like a shelf.

Nadia frowned and grabbed the ruler. She laid it along the top edge of her frontmost window and drew a new line, dead horizontal. Then she checked the doorframe, erased the tilted one, and drew it straight up and down. The second shop, farther back, she left slanted toward the dot. She held the page up at arm's length. "The fronts standing straight make the whole street look like it goes back forever," she said. "The leaning ones made my eyes hurt."

Owen pulled his page back over and got to work. He drew his street, then ruled the fronts of the near buildings so the window tops stayed perfectly horizontal and the doorframes stayed perfectly vertical, and only the side walls ran inward toward his dot. He began to elaborate on the bakery, adding a door handle, a chalkboard sign, and a crack in the pavement that narrowed as it went. He was so absorbed that he didn't notice the green fuzz on the bread he'd been nibbling until Nadia pointed at it.

"Your crust has fungus," she said.

Owen slid the bread away and kept drawing, his pencil moving in assertive, confident strokes. "Vanishing point," he said, tapping the dot. "You still need me to explain it to you?"

The community hall smelled like coffee and floor wax, and Aiden spread his poster board across two folding tables near the window. His project for the interfaith fair was supposed to compare how two faiths explained what happens after death, and he had picked his grandmother's Catholic church and his friend Marcus's church, which was Baptist. Marcus arrived carrying a box of markers, his church's laminated flyer tucked under his arm. "My pastor says when you die, if you believe, you go straight to heaven," Marcus said. "That's it. Straight up."

Aiden frowned at his notes. "That's not what Sister Rosalind told me on Sunday." He flipped a page and read aloud. "She said Catholics believe in a state of purification after death, before heaven. She called it purgatory."

Marcus set down the markers. "Pur what?"

That had pushed Aiden out the door with his notebook, and he had interviewed Sister Rosalind, then Mr. Okafor from the Baptist church, then Marcus's aunt.

The two boys stared at the notes. "So both churches are Christian," Marcus said slowly, "and both believe in heaven, but the Catholic one has this middle place and mine doesn't?"

Aiden pulled out two sticky notes and a toy car. "Let me demonstrate what I mean." He stuck HEAVEN on the far wall and SOUL on the toy car. "In your church, the car drives straight there." He rolled it across the table. "In the Catholic Church, it stops at a cleaning station first." He stuck a third note that read PURGATORY in the middle of the route.

"That's actually a good diagram," Marcus admitted. Then he grinned. "I want to draw the car. I do better cars than you."

They worked until the hall lights flickered, Marcus drawing a little car with flames of scrubbing bubbles around it, Aiden rewriting his comparison chart so both columns got equal space. When his grandmother came to pick him up, she read the whole poster twice.

"You didn't tilt it toward us," she said.

"I tried not to," Aiden said. "Same questions, same size boxes."

She tapped the purgatory sticky note. "I like the car."

Marcus held up the marker. "He gets the chart, I get the car. Deal?"

"Deal," Aiden said, and rolled the toy car one more time, straight through the middle station and home.

Florence had exactly one lunch period to fix her essay outline, because Ms. Ruiz collected drafts at the start of sixth period. She spread her papers across the library table and glared at her thesis statement as if it were an adversary in a wrestling match: "Our school should restrict cell phone use to the office, because phones distract students, upset teachers, and make cheating easy."

Her best friend Dana slid into the chair across from her with a sandwich and a buoyant grin. "You look like your outline bit you."

"It did." Florence tapped her three body paragraph notes. "I wrote the distraction paragraph first, but then I switched. My cheating evidence is way stronger, so I moved it up. Now the paragraphs go cheating, distraction, upset teachers."

"So? Just fix the thesis."

Florence stared at the sentence. "Wait." She read it again, then read her paragraph order again, then read the thesis a third time, her finger tracking each word. The thesis listed distract, upset, cheat. The paragraphs now went cheat, distract, upset. They were opposites, like a map pointing north while she walked south.

"Dana. The thesis has to name the points in the same order the paragraphs talk about them."

"Why would order matter? It's the same three points."

"I don't know why. It just does. Look." Florence grabbed a pencil, flipped her thesis paper over, and wrote the points as three quick headings in her new order. Then she tried it out like an experiment. She read the old thesis, then the headings. "Phones make cheating easy, distract students, and upset teachers." Same ideas, different order. Then she laid the headings beside it, one by one, matching them like a card game she used to play with her grandmother. First card matched first point. Second matched second. Third matched third. When she tried it against her original thesis, the matches crossed each other like tangled shoelaces.

"Okay," Dana said, chewing. "That's actually satisfying."

Florence erased the old thesis and wrote the new one, keeping the same order all the way down. She numbered her outline points to match, one, two, three, then checked it twice, covering each heading with her hand and saying it from memory. The bell for fifth period rang while she was still checking.

She crammed the papers into her binder, and Dana held the door. "Sixth period," Dana said. "You'll make it."

Florence ran down the hall with the binder hugged to her chest, feeling the clean order of it, one, two, three, all the way to room 214.

The line at St. Benedict's gymnasium snaked past the bake sale table, and Lea stood in the middle of it holding her notebook like a shield. Her assignment was due Monday: pick one right from Canada's Charter of Rights and Freedoms, read it carefully, and explain it in her own words. The problem was that every time she tried, her explanation came out sounding exactly like the original, just with the words in a different order, like a pizza with the toppings shuffled.

"Move up, Lea, you're letting in a draft," said her mother, who was working the registration table in a volunteer badge that said ELECTION OFFICIAL, though she kept calling herself "the pencil dictator." Today was also Take Our Kids to Work day, sort of, since the school had decided the polling station counted as a field trip. Lea was supposed to participate, which her teacher had said with the solemnity of someone announcing a mission to Mars.

"You could interview voters," her mother suggested. "Ask them what right they'd fight for."

Lea tried it on the man in the green scarf. He said parking. She tried it on a woman with a wheeled walker, who said the right to a decent spot in line, which at least had something to do with fairness. Then a boy her age, Jonas from her geography class, turned up beside his father, looking as bored as she felt.

"My cousins live in Germany," Jonas said, apropos of nothing, the way he did. "I looked up their constitution once, the Basic Law, just to compare it with ours. Want to know how theirs starts? Not with freedom of speech, not with voting. Article 1 says, 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.' First thing. Before everything else."

"Inviolable," Lea repeated. "Like, un-breakable."

"Like your mom's lemon squares, maybe," Jonas said, and his father shushed him, but Lea was already writing. She had expected something sinister lurking in constitutions, long clauses like camouflage hiding the real meaning, but this was the opposite: the plainest sentence she'd read all week.

She tested an idea on the next voter, an elderly woman in a raincoat. "If someone made you explain 'human dignity shall be inviolable' without using any of those words, what would you say?"

The woman thought about it. "I'd say nobody gets to treat me like a thing. Not the government, not my landlord, not anybody. Not ever."

Lea wrote it down, then crossed it out and made it hers: You can't turn a person into something less than a person, and no law is allowed to change that. She read it to Jonas.

"Better than my mark's going to be," he said. "I wrote mine about parking."

"You did not."

"My dad might have influenced me." His father voted, got his "I Voted" sticker, and put it on Jonas's forehead like a medal.

Lea turned to the next person in line, notebook open, pencil ready. "Excuse me, can I ask you one question about dignity?"

story:
Madison had won the hundred metres at every meet since sixth grade, so when Coach Ruiz posted the relay team for Saturday and left her off it, replacing her with the eight hundred, she read the sheet three times before her face got hot. "It's not a punishment," Coach said, already walking away. "Just try it once."

At practice the next afternoon, the track was striped with white lanes and an ominous bank of grey clouds sat over the far bleachers. Madison planned to run it like she ran everything, which was all at once, from the gun. She went through the first lap in sixty-two seconds, four seconds faster than her training times, and she felt magnificent right up until the back straight of the second lap, when her legs turned to something that did not belong to her. She finished stumbling, in last place among the practice group, and stood with her hands on her knees while the grey clouds finally broke and rain started dotting the rubber.

Denise, who ran the mile and never seemed to tire, jogged over and offered her water bottle. "You went out too fast," Denise said. "Everyone does, their first time."

"Fast is the whole point," Madison said. "I'm a sprinter."

Denise shook her head. "The eight hundred isn't a sprint. But it's not really a distance race either. It's both at once." She squinted at the sky. "Coach says it burns two kinds of fuel. One of them needs oxygen, and that one lasts. The other one works without oxygen, but it runs out fast. You just spent all of yours on lap one."

Madison turned that over all through dinner and again on the bus to school. Two fuel tanks, she thought. She'd emptied the quick one in sixty seconds flat. The way she'd felt on that back straight, the dead legs and the roaring chest, was what empty looked like. But nobody could watch a fuel tank drain, so the only way to manage it was to watch something she could see. The clock. If she held a steady pace instead of burning everything at the start, maybe the second tank would still have something in it when the race turned into a fight.

She decided to invest one whole practice in the experiment. If it failed, she'd waste an afternoon, but if the dead legs were really caused by going out too hard, and not just by the race being impossible, then slowing down early would actually make her faster at the end.

Saturday came cold and bright. The starter raised the pistol. Madison let the pack surge ahead of her, and every metre of that first lap felt wrong, felt like losing, felt like an embarrassment waiting for her at the finish line. She counted her steps and hung on. Four hundred metres. Two hundred. At the top of the final curve, Denise was ten metres ahead and slowing, and Madison still had legs.

She passed Denise with sixty metres to go, and this time the legs were hers.

"Where did that come from?" Denise gasped at the line.

"Fuel," Madison said, and bent over, laughing into her knees.

"First the onion," his mom had said from the car window. "Cut it in half from top to root, then lay each half flat side down so it can't roll. Hold it with the claw grip. Fingertips tucked in, knuckles forward." He had waved her off, but now he wished he'd paid more attention.

He set the onion on the cutting board and positioned his knife near the middle. The onion rocked, round and smug. He tried again, and it rolled three inches to the left, nearly off the counter. Okay. He thought about what she'd said. Cut it in half from top to root. He lined the blade up with the hairy root end and pressed down hard. The knife went through with a crack, and the onion split into two halves. He lay one half flat side down, and it sat there. Completely still. He nudged it with the knife tip. It didn't move. The flat side was the answer. It couldn't roll because it had a steady base now. He felt a little jolt of triumph and immediately felt silly about it.

The onion still intimidated him, though. He curled his fingers into a claw, knuckles bent forward like tiny shields, and brought the blade down in slow slices. It worked. His fingertips were nowhere near the edge. His eyes burned, so he worked faster, and the pieces came out uneven, some thick slabs, some near-transparent wisps. Fine. It would all cook down anyway.

He heated olive oil in the big pot, added the onion, and listened to it sizzle. While it softened, he crushed the canned tomatoes with his hands, which was more fun than he'd expected. Garlic, a pinch of sugar, salt, a long stir. He tasted it at the four-minute mark and frowned. Bland. He'd been planning to surprise Nonna by having it perfect, ready, untouchable. Now he added more salt, stirred, tasted again. Better. He decided right then that he'd let her adjust it herself, and that maybe that was even a nicer welcome than perfection.

At five fifty-two the sauce was bubbling gently, a small, careful ecosystem of tomatoes and onion and oil that he had built from nothing. The kitchen smelled like her kitchen. When the door opened, Nonna set down her bag and inhaled. "Who has been cooking?" Carter wiped his hands on the towel. "Me. But it needs something." She rolled up her sleeves and lifted the lid. "It needs you to stir it, and me to watch," she said, handing him the wooden spoon.

Her project was due Monday: compare a desert city and a rainforest city using rainfall bars and temperature lines. On paper it looked easy. It was Marcus, her tutor, calling in from the library. "You stuck?" he asked.

"Not really," Arianna said, turning the laptop so he could see the table. "It's obvious. Singapore's bars are taller, so it's wetter."

"Before you write that, check the numbers on the side of each graph," Marcus said. "Just check them."

She leaned close to the paper. Cairo's rainfall axis climbed to twenty millimeters. Singapore's climbed to four hundred. She sat back, then pulled the sheets nearer, running her finger up the thin printed lines. The tallest bar on Cairo's graph stood for about five millimeters of rain. "That's the trap with these," Marcus said. "Two climate graphs can only be compared by bar height if their rainfall axes use the same scale."

"So the graphs are lying?" Her younger brother, Devon, had wandered in for crackers and was now looking over her shoulder, chewing.

"They're not lying, they're just not matching," Arianna said. She was already scribbling on the back of an envelope, adding up Cairo's twelve monthly bars and then Singapore's. The room smelled like the printer's warm ink, and her sock had snagged on a splinter in the floorboard, but she barely moved. Marcus was watching from the screen. "So what are you going to write?"

Amelia burst through the door of the community room with her copy of The Monkey's Paw flapping in one hand. "I found something," she announced, dropping into the circle of folding chairs. "Remember the sergeant?"

Mr. White snatches the paw out of the flames, and that's the exact moment he chooses not to listen."

Priya sat up straight. "So the warning isn't hidden at all. It's a whole man throwing a whole object into a fire, in front of everybody." She grabbed her own copy and found the scene, running her finger down the lines. "He even says the results are terrible. Wow. "If the paw were just evil, the warning wouldn't matter. But if the story is telling us cause and effect, then every wish after that is like Herbert knocking on the door at the end. "Okay," he said. "Tomorrow I'm bringing a list of every warning in the story. Race you to find the most."

story:
Grandpa slid a folded paper across the kitchen table, next to the plate of oatmeal cookies he had set out the moment John walked in. "Read it before Sunday dinner," he said. "That's the deadline. After that, the offer's off the table."

The paper said that Grandpa would hold John's $1,000 for five years at 5 percent simple interest. At the bottom, in shaky pencil, he had written "treaty" and drawn a line for two signatures, like the boys were signing an agreement between nations.

"That's not how banks work," John said.

"Good," said Grandpa. "Then you'd better find out how they do."

John's objective was simple: figure out which deal left him richer in five years. That night he sat at the desk in the spare room, the one that still smelled of Grandma's lavender, and spread out his notebook. The simple part was easy. Five percent of $1,000 was $50, and it was $50 every year, the same flat amount, never more. After five years, Grandpa's envelope would hold $1,250. He wrote it in big numbers and boxed it.

The bank part was harder, because compound interest didn't add the same amount each year. The interest earned its own interest, so the pile grew a little faster every year. John ran his finger down the bank's brochure, muttering to himself until his little cousin Mia, who was staying the week, leaned in the doorway.

"What are you doing?"

"I'll narrate," John said, tapping his pencil. "Year one, fifty dollars. Year two, the fifty earns interest too, so it's a bit more than fifty. It keeps going like that. By year five, the bank account beats Grandpa's deal."

"By how much?"

"Twenty-six dollars. Roughly."

Mia slid into the chair beside him and turned the notebook so she could see. "Twenty-six dollars is a lot of candy," she said, and she copied his boxes onto her own sheet of paper, carefully, the way she did everything.

Sunday dinner was roast chicken, and Grandpa carved in silence until John pushed his notebook across the tablecloth. "I did the math. Your deal ends at $1,250. The bank's compound account ends at $1,276. So I'm going with the bank."

Grandpa set down the knife, wiped his hands, and smiled at Mia. "You want the treaty, sweetheart? He was right about every number."

Mia signed her name in big loops, and Grandpa matched it, and John felt his ears go warm, because twenty-six dollars was twenty-six dollars and he had won the math fair and square.

"Which bank were you going to use?" Grandpa asked, ladling gravy.

"The one on Maple. Five percent, compounded."

Grandpa shook his head slowly and reached for another piece of chicken. "Maple Street dropped to three percent in March, John. You were reading last year's brochure."

Mia looked up from the treaty, pencil still in her hand. "So his account ends at $1,159," she said, "and mine ends at $1,250."

Grandpa held out the gravy to John. "More chicken?"

story:
Nicolas had forty minutes before the community centre's math room closed for the night, and the booklet in front of him still showed three unsolved equations. The tutor had already left, and the front desk clerk had made it clear that only students who signed the attendance sheet before nine o'clock would be authorized to use the room again next week. He had missed the sign-in once already. If he missed it again, his mother would find out he was skipping tutoring, and his mother was notorious for finding things out first.

The first equation was x + 7 = 19. That one he could do in his head. The second was 4x - 5 = 27, and the third, 3x + 12 = 2x + 20, made him put his pencil down. The scale was balanced, his tutor kept saying, like a boat whose hull sits level in the water; whatever you did to one side, you had to do to the other, or the whole thing tipped. Nicolas understood the words. He just didn't trust them.

He turned the booklet over. On the back page, in his grandfather's looping handwriting, there was a note from last Sunday, when Nicolas had complained about homework at the kitchen table. His grandfather had drawn two short parallel lines and written: "Who do you think first made this sign? Robert Recorde, a Welsh mathematician, in 1557. He picked two parallel lines because no two things could be more equal." Nicolas had laughed at the time. Now he stared at the two little lines and thought about them differently. If the lines were parallel, they never crossed, never diverged, never stopped matching.

"All right," he whispered. "If they're that equal, then whatever I throw at one side, I throw at the other."

He tested it on the hard equation. Both sides had an x, and that bothered him because he couldn't see x at all, only the numbers around it, like wake behind a boat hiding the hull. But the hidden thing, he reasoned, had to follow the visible rule. He subtracted 2x from the right side, so he subtracted 2x from the left side too. The equation became x + 12 = 20. Then he subtracted 12 from both sides, and there it was, plain as anything: x = 8. He checked it by putting 8 back into the original. Twenty-four plus twelve equaled sixteen plus twenty. Both sides came to thirty-six. The two lines held.

The clock over the door said 8:52. Nicolas signed the attendance sheet, slid it across the desk to the clerk, and copied the third equation onto a scrap of paper to show his grandfather on Sunday. At the door he stopped, pulled the scrap back out of his pocket, and added one line beneath the numbers: two short parallel lines, drawn slowly and carefully, twice as long as they needed to be.

The deadline was four o'clock, and Arianna had until then to prove her entry for the memorial's young historians contest deserved a spot on the display table. Her topic was why families moved west in the 1800s, and the judge, a gray-haired woman named Mrs. Okafor, had circled a note on her first draft: "Use a primary source, not just your textbook."

Arianna spread her materials on the bench beside the stone wall where the names of soldiers were carved. She had her textbook, published six years ago, full of neat paragraphs about land and opportunity. She also had the photocopies the memorial's archive volunteer had slid across the counter an hour ago: pages from a diary kept by a woman named Hannah Pierce, who had walked a trail in 1852 with her husband and three children.

She read the diary pages again, hunting. One line stopped her. Hannah had written that her husband's crops had failed two springs in a row and the bank had taken half the farm, so they would try the western land before winter. Two failed springs. A bank. Arianna had never seen that in the textbook, which said people went west "seeking opportunity." That word covered everything and explained nothing. The diary showed the actual reason, from a person it had actually happened to.

"You look like you're arguing with that page," said Devon, her younger brother, who had been tracing soldiers' names with a pencil and paper like a nocturnal creature finally dragged into daylight.

"I'm figuring out which one counts." She held up the photocopy. "This is a primary source. A settler's diary, made at the time by a person who lived through it." She tapped the textbook. "This is a secondary source, written later by someone studying it."

"So the diary wins."

"The diary wins."

She tested the idea to be sure. Could the textbook author have been there in 1852? No, it was written more than a century and a half later. Could Hannah Pierce have been lying about the bank? Maybe, but she wrote it as it happened, in ink, on the trail, and that was exactly what Mrs. Okafor wanted: not a summary, but evidence. An idea began to germinate in Arianna's head. She could build her whole display around the diary, quote it directly, and use the textbook only as a background voice.

She copied Hannah's sentence onto a card in her best handwriting, then found one more anecdote deeper in the stack: Hannah's daughter had traded her hair ribbons to a wagon train scout for extra flour. Small, real, something no textbook would bother to print.

At three fifty, Arianna carried her cards to the display table. Mrs. Okafor picked up the first one, read the quoted line, and looked up.

"Who took the farm?"

"The bank," Arianna said. "She wrote it herself."

story:
The fire drill poster outside the science lab had a cartoon flame and the word flammable in capital letters, and Naomi had walked past it every day for three weeks without reading the rest. Today she stopped, because stopping and noticing small things was part of the plan in her health class notebook. The plan had three lines: notice what stress feels like, breathe four counts in and six counts out, and protect her sleep. Her teacher had not explained the last one much, which was why it interested her most.

At lunch, Marcus slammed his tray down so hard that his juice tipped. Dev had taken one of his fries, the way he did every single day, and Marcus told him to knock it off with his jaw tight and his voice too loud. Dev put his hands up. "It's one fry, man. You usually just throw fries at me back."

"He's been weird since the science fair," Priya said after Marcus stomped off to the far table. "He told me he was up all of Tuesday night finishing his volcano display. Like, no sleep at all."

Naomi turned that over. Marcus and Dev traded fries all the time. It was practically a ritual. One bad night should not turn a joke into a crisis, unless something invisible was going on. She had a working idea: maybe missing sleep made people react more strongly to small annoyances, the way dry wood catches easier than green wood. That would make sleep itself a factor in how a day went, and it was the kind of thing a person could actually test.

That evening she found her mother's laptop open to an article about sleep, and one line stopped her cold. She read it twice, then copied it into her notebook word for word: In a 2007 study, people kept awake for a whole night showed about 60 percent stronger reactions to upsetting pictures in the amygdala, a brain area that responds to threats. Sixty percent. She showed Priya the notebook the next morning in the hallway. "It's called the amygdala," Naomi said, pointing at the underlined word. "A brain area that responds to threats. So when Marcus flipped out over a fry, his brain was basically seeing a bigger threat than the fry really was."

"So he wasn't just being a jerk," Priya said.

"He was running on a whole night of no sleep, and his brain turned everything up about sixty percent. Mine would too." Naomi felt her own shoulders drop as she said it, and she did one slow breath, four counts in and six counts out, right there by the lockers.

They found Marcus before first period. Priya told him about the study, and Naomi read the sentence aloud from her notebook. Marcus listened with his arms folded, then uncrossed them. "I have a huge history test Friday," he said. "I was going to stay up until two studying."

"Don't," Naomi said. She flipped to her plan page and held it out. "Try this instead. Breathe like this, and go to bed at ten."

Marcus looked at the page, then folded his hands over his stomach, breathed in for four, and let it out slow for six.

Juliette had forty minutes until fifth period, and Mrs. Okafor's quiz was supposed to be easy if you had actually done the reading, which Juliette had, twice, without any of it sticking.

"A stock is part ownership of one company," she recited to Priya as they sat on the gymnasium steps. "A bond is a loan that gets paid back. That part I can say in my sleep. The part I can't say is which one is riskier and why."

Priya peeled the label off her water bottle in one long strip. "My uncle lost a bunch of money once because he put everything in one airline stock. Then the company crashed and that was that."

"And your cousin?"

"My cousin had money in a thing that held a bunch of different stocks. The same airline was in there. When it crashed, she barely noticed."

Juliette stopped chewing her granola bar. "Wait. Same crash, same company. One of them got wrecked and one of them basically yawned?"

"Basically."

"That's the whole quiz, isn't it." Juliette dug out her notebook and wrote airline, uncle, everything, wrecked. Then fund, cousin, lots of stocks, fine. She stared at the two lines like they might confess something. "So the danger isn't the stock itself. It's having all your money riding on one company."

"It has a name," Priya said. "Diversifying."

"Of course it does." Juliette wrote the word down and underlined it twice, which was the most respect she had ever paid a vocabulary term. "Okay, so I have to verify this before I write it down as the answer and get it wrong anyway. Who else do we know who owns anything?"

"Dmitri's brother works at the bank. He's basically the ambassador of boring money stuff. He'll talk about it forever if you let him."

They found Dmitri in the cafeteria, and Dmitri texted his brother, and the answer came back in under a minute: Yeah, diversifying means one company's collapse hurts way less than if all the money were in that one stock. Tell your friend to stop panicking.

"I wasn't panicking," Juliette said, panicking a little less now. She copied the sentence into her notebook word for word, because Mrs. Okafor gave partial credit for precision and Juliette needed every fragment of it. "So on the quiz, the answer is that a single stock can be riskier, and I can prove it with the uncle and the cousin."

"The uncle's going to love being your homework," Priya said.

"He's the endangered species of this story. One crash and he was gone." Juliette capped her pen. The bell rang. She gathered her things, read the sentence one more time, and walked toward room 214 saying, "Wrecked and yawning. I can work with that."

Colton had one hour before the bus left the pioneer museum, and one worksheet with a blank line where his answer was supposed to go. The question read: "Using the diary of Sarah Pruitt, explain why her family left Missouri in 1846." He stared at the glass case holding a leather-bound diary, open to a page of faded brown ink, and next to it a typed card with the words printed out.

His friend Marisol leaned over his shoulder. "Just copy something about free land," she whispered.

"That's not an answer, that's a guess." Colton read the card slowly. Some lines were easy to picture: the river flooded their bottom field twice in three years, and the price of corn kept falling. Other lines were dreams: reports of rich soil in the Willamette Valley, and a letter from an uncle who had gone ahead and said the winters were mild. Sarah had also written that her father could not pass up "a fresh start," though her mother cried the night they sold the plow and the milk cow.

The museum's docent, an old man polishing a brass valve from a steam engine in the next room, caught Colton frowning. "Trouble?"

"I can't tell if they left because things were bad or because Oregon sounded good. It's both. How do I put both on one line?"

"That puzzle has a handle," the man said, and pointed his polishing cloth at a wall chart. Colton walked over. The chart showed a map with arrows: "Historians sort reasons for migration into push factors, which drive people away from home, and pull factors, which attract them to a new place."

Colton read it twice. "Push and pull," he said. "So the floods and the falling corn prices pushed the Pruitts out of Missouri, and the soil and the uncle's letter pulled them west."

"Sounds like you could test it," the docent said. "Go line by line. Every reason goes in one pile or the other."

Colton sat on the bench by the case and made two lists in his notebook. Flood: push. Falling corn prices: push. Rich soil: pull. Uncle's letter: pull. His first draft had just said "they wanted free land," which now looked thin and lazy, so he revised it into two sentences, one for each pile. Marisol checked his lists against the card and tapped the mother crying. "Which one is that?"

Colton thought. Crying wasn't a reason to go or stay, exactly; it was what leaving cost. He decided that was true too, and wrote it last. When the whistle blew for the bus, he closed his notebook and looked back at the diary in its case, the ink still saying the same things it had said for a hundred and fifty years.

"Thanks," he told the docent, holding up the worksheet, both lines full.

story:
Grandpa's periodic table hung on the wall behind the kitchen table, its squares faded to the color of old lemonade. Andrew had eaten breakfast under it every summer since he was six, and he had never once read it. This morning he pulled his chair closer, because his science teacher had promised a quiz on the first twenty elements when school started, and Andrew had a reason to care: whoever scored highest got to help run the wind turbine demo at the school's energy fair, and Andrew had been waiting two years for that job.

"The atomic number tells you the protons," Grandpa said, sliding a magnifying glass across the table. "That's all I'm giving you. The rest you find yourself." He went back to his coffee, which was his permanent answer to most questions before seven in the morning.

Andrew traced the numbers with his finger. Hydrogen, 1. Helium, 2. Carbon, 6. He counted protons the way he counted laps in the pool, one square at a time, until he hit a snag. Helium sat at the far right edge, but neon and argon sat under it in a neat line, all the way down the table. He leaned back. "Why is helium over there with the big guys? Hydrogen's alone on the left."

Grandpa only raised an eyebrow, so Andrew had to evaluate the situation himself. He ran his finger down the column. Helium, neon, argon, krypton. Every one of them. He remembered his uncle's birthday balloons floating to the ceiling, the neon sign in the diner window that glowed even in daylight, and the time Grandpa had shown him old light bulbs with argon inside. All of them just sat there, quiet, not mixing with anything, not rusting or burning.

"Grandpa, what do you call the columns? The up-and-down ones?"

"Groups," Grandpa said. "The vertical columns are called groups."

Andrew tapped the table. "So elements in the same group act alike. That's why they're stacked together." It was like finding out the kids who sat together at lunch were actually cousins. He tested it on another column, lithium and sodium, and remembered Grandpa's story about a chunk of sodium dropped in a pond back in 1968, spitting fire across the water. Grandpa had laughed telling it last summer, though he'd also said he still wasn't sure he should have done it, and Andrew had never decided whether that made the story better or worse.

"Nine protons," Andrew said, tapping fluorine. "Ten for neon. Eight for oxygen." The quiz suddenly felt like a scavenger hunt instead of a trap. He copied the first twenty numbers onto an index card, then flipped it over and drew the groups as tall towers, each one a family with its own habits.

Grandpa looked at the towers and then at Andrew. "You know," he said, "I failed chemistry in 1954 because nobody told me the table was a map. They just made me memorize the exits." He set down his cup. "Fifteen protons, boy. Which element?"

Andrew grinned and tapped phosphorus. "Right there. Same column as nitrogen."

He tested it on carbon, then on oxygen, flipping the key open after each one like a magician checking his own trick.

"Judges love it when you emphasize the math," Priya said, straightening a graph. "Mr. Ruiz says the whole fair is basically a democracy of clipboards. They vote."

"Thanks. That helps zero percent."

The judge reached Adam's table. "Walk me through your model," she said, and Adam began, pointing out the protons and electrons. Then she tapped the foam core. "How many neutrons are in there, and how do you know?"

Adam's mouth went dry, the way it had at the spelling bee. But this time he had the rule, not a guess. "Oxygen's atomic number is eight, so eight protons," he said. "Its mass number is sixteen. Sixteen minus eight is eight neutrons." He picked up the periodic table he'd taped beside the poster and ran his finger across the row. "It works for any element. You don't have to look the neutrons up."

The judge wrote something. Outside the gym doors, a turbulent spring wind rattled the banners hung from the rafters, and one corner of Adam's poster lifted, threatening to peel away entirely. He slammed his palm down on it and held it flat while she asked her next question.

story:
The dome of the planetarium was still dark from the last show when Hailey slipped in through the side door, a flashlight in one hand and her brother's globe in the other. In three days she had to explain the seasons to her science class, and she still could not make it work. Every time she pictured Earth going around the Sun, she imagined the whole planet getting warmer in summer because it was closer, which Mr. Ruiz had marked wrong with a big red circle.

She set the globe on the demonstration table near the plumbing that piped warm water under the seats, because the tabletop there was widest. The dome above her was tranquil, a faint scatter of leftover stars still glowing on its ceiling. She switched on the flashlight and held it level, like a Sun.

"Okay," she whispered. "Tilt the top toward the light. Northern hemisphere, summer." She walked the globe halfway around the table, keeping the flashlight aimed at it, and tilted the top away. "Winter." But when she looked at the two bright patches, they looked the same size, and she felt the same sinking feeling she'd had when her poster got the red circle.

Then she remembered something from July. At summer camp, her counselor had called lights-out at nine, and it had still been light enough outside to read a comic through the tent mesh. Her bedtime had come before dark. She frowned and turned the globe back to the tilt-toward position.

The flashlight beam spread across the northern half, and something else caught her eye. She grabbed a marker and laid it flat along the table edge, then slowly spun the globe, watching the flashlight. When the north was tilted toward the light, the lit half of the northern half stayed lit longer than the dark half stayed dark. The days stretched. The Sun had more hours to warm the ground.

"That's it," she said out loud, then clapped a hand over her mouth because a voice echoed from the control booth.

"What's it?" called Dara, the student volunteer, climbing down the steps with a bag of chips.

"Longer days," Hailey said. "The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets longer days, so sunlight has more hours to warm the ground. That's the part I was missing."

Dara crunched a chip and leaned over the globe. "So when it's tilted away?"

Hailey spun the globe slowly, marker in hand, watching the shadow creep up the northern half far too soon.

"Try it," she said, and held out the flashlight.

story:
The assignment was due Monday morning: build a model that shows how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, and explain it to the class without notes. Florence had put it off all week, and now it was Sunday, and the only place she could work was her grandpa's backyard, where he was still trying to pay off the mortgage on the house and kept every scrap of lumber for a reason.

"You need a slope," Grandpa said, propping a long wooden tray on two bricks so one end sat higher than the other. "Rivers don't sit flat." He watched her dump in a bucket of soil mixed with gravel from the driveway, pebbles and grit and fine dust all jumbled together. "There's your land. Now find your river."

Floorce turned the hose on slow. A thin ribbon of water crept down the tray and barely moved anything. She frowned and opened the valve wider. The current quickened, and suddenly pebbles began to slide and tumble along with the mud, the whole load racing downhill. "It's carrying the big rocks," she said. "I didn't think it could."

At the bottom of the tray the water spread out into a wide, shallow pan, and there Florence noticed something odd. The pebbles had stopped first, piled right where the tray met the pan, while the grit had traveled farther and the finest mud drifted all the way to the far edge of the water, hanging there in a luminous brown cloud before settling. She knelt down and ran her finger along the bottom. Coarse, then medium, then smooth silt, neat as stripes on a cake. "Grandpa, look. The big stuff landed first." She tried it again with the hose wide, then narrow, and got the same result both times. When the water moved fast it hauled everything along, and the moment it slowed, it dropped what it carried, and the largest pieces settled out first.

"That's deposition," she said, writing it on her poster with a fat marker, "when the river slows down and drops its load." Underneath she drew a cross-section of her tray, arrows showing pebbles stopping at the top of the pan and mud settling last at the bottom. The canyon part she showed with a second run: she let the hose pour down the same channel for half an hour, and though the groove was tiny, it was deeper at the end than at the start, and she wrote "multiply by millions of years" beside a photo of the real Grand Canyon taped to the corner.

Grandpa sat beside her on the porch steps as the sun went down, and the last light caught the muddy water in the pan so it glowed like a small amber lake. "You know, when I was twelve I would have just drawn a picture and hoped," he said. "You tested it."

Florence held up the poster so he could see the striped layers drawn in careful colored pencil. "Fast water carries the big stuff, slow water drops it, and the big stuff always lands first," she said. "Go on, quiz me."

"Tomorrow, after your presentation," Grandpa said, and reached over to turn off the hose.
