story:
Sara's science grade was riding on Friday's presentation, and she still could not say why summer was hot and winter was cold without mumbling something about "the Sun being closer," which Mr. Okafor had already crossed out in red pen. Her old partner, Denise, would have made a poster and a joke and carried them both through. But Denise's family had moved in October, and the seat beside Sara had stayed empty so long that the room felt desolate whenever she looked at it.

At lunch she dragged the classroom globe to the windowsill and spun it slowly, hunting for anything that might help. Two dotted lines circled the globe, one above the equator and one below it. She traced the top one with her finger and read the tiny label out loud. "Tropic of Cancer."

"That's the one where the Sun is straight overhead in June," said Marcus, who had been stacking chairs and now leaned on the radiator, which radiated a dry heat that made the whole room smell like dust. "My grandpa told me. Around June twenty-first, at noon, the Sun is directly overhead right there. Around December twenty-first, it's directly overhead at the other dotted one."

"The Tropic of Capricorn," Sara said, spinning the globe to find it below the equator.

"That's the one," Marcus said. "He farmed his whole life, and he knew the sky better than anybody. A peasant with no schooling, he called himself, but he could tell you what the Sun would do on any day of the year."

Sara went home and thought about it on the bus, her forehead against the cold window. Not closer, then. Overhead, but in different places at different times of year. She decided to test it.

In her room she set the globe on her desk and turned off the lamp, then clicked on her flashlight. She held the beam straight down over the Tropic of Cancer and looked at the patch of light it made, small and intense, all that brightness crowded onto a little circle of ocean. Then she tilted the beam toward the equator, the way the light would have to come from somewhere farther from that spot, and the patch stretched into a long oval, the same light spread thin across a whole stretch of sea and land. She moved the flashlight down over the Tropic of Capricorn and did it again, watching the oval slide from one hemisphere to the other. She drew what she saw in her notebook: circle, oval, circle, oval, her pencil moving fast enough to tear a corner of the page.

On Friday she carried the globe and the flashlight to the front of the class, and her hands shook only a little. She shined the light straight down on the top dotted line and said, "Around June twenty-first, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer." She moved the beam to the bottom line. "Around December twenty-first, it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn." Then she showed the crowd of light and the stretched oval, and she watched understanding move across the faces in the second row.

Afterward Mr. Okafor wrote a check plus at the top of her rubric, and Marcus caught her eye from across the room and raised one fist, grinning. But there was no note passed under the desk afterward, no voice in her ear saying "we crushed it," the way Denise used to. Sara slid the rubric into her binder, careful not to bend the corner, and carried the globe back to its stand by herself.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
story:
Chase stood in his grandfather's study on Sunday morning, staring at the open Torah scroll on the desk. In three weeks he would chant his bar mitzvah portion in front of everyone, and so far he could only get through four lines without his mind wandering off like a dog after a squirrel.

"Again," his grandfather said, settling into the chair beside him. "Start at the shema."

Chase began, and the Hebrew letters marched along the parchment, some fat, some thin, some crowned with little hooks. His voice wobbled on the sixth line. He leaned closer, squinting, and his finger drifted toward the scroll to keep his place.

His grandfather caught his wrist, gentle but quick, and pressed something into his palm instead. It was a slim silver rod, about as long as a pencil, shaped like a tiny hand at the tip. "A yad," his grandfather said. "The word means hand."

Chase turned it over, wondering why he needed a fake hand when he had two real ones right there. Was it just decoration, like the fancy curtains in this room? He decided to test it. He held the yad's tip just above the line he was reading, and something odd happened: the words stopped sliding around. His eye had an anchor. He read line six, then line seven, then line eleven, and his voice did not wobble once.

He tried the next line with his own finger hovering instead, close but not touching, and the letters seemed to blur back into a crowd of lookalikes. Why would a metal hand work better than his own? Maybe it was thinner and pointed, so it marked exactly one word instead of a whole blurry fingertip. Or maybe the silver stood out against the tan parchment the way a red thread stands out on a white shirt. His brain felt like it was lighting up one neuron at a time, firing small sparks of figuring out.

Whatever the reason, his improvement was not a sudden miracle but a gradual settling, like water going still. His grandfather watched, smiling a little, saying nothing.

"Can I try the whole portion?" Chase asked.

"Go ahead," his grandfather said. "From the top."

Chase laid the little silver hand on the first word and began.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
story:
Penelope jabbed her pencil at her drawing and groaned. "My street looks like a brick wall with lampposts glued on it."

Marcus leaned over from the next stool. "At least your lampposts match. Mine look like a family of wobbly golf umbrellas."

The assignment was a street scene in one-point perspective, and Penelope had done everything Mr. Ruiz had put on the board. She had drawn the vanishing point dead center, then the road edges as diagonal lines zooming toward it, then buildings leaning in on both sides. The road even looked like it went somewhere. But her lampposts, all six of them marching down the sidewalk, stood exactly the same height with exactly the same gap between them, and together they flattened the whole page. She held the drawing at arm's length and squinted. Wall. Total wall.

"Wait," she said. "Look at the road edges." The two lines squeezed closer and closer as they ran toward the vanishing point, like the road itself was shrinking. "If the road gets smaller in the distance, the lampposts should shrink too. They're the same real size out there, but far away they have to take up less space on the paper."

"So just make the back ones shorter?" Marcus said. "Won't that look broken?"

Penelope didn't answer. She grabbed a fresh sheet and sketched fast: road, vanishing point, then lampposts that started tall at the front edge and stepped down shorter and shorter, and closer together too, until the last one was a little stub near the vanishing point. She held it up. The street stretched back into the paper like a hallway. "Whoa. It goes."

"That's actually creepy," Marcus said. "I feel like I could walk into it and hit your vanishing point with my face."

"Try it," Penelope said, and slid her spare pencil down the diagonal curb line like a tiny skateboard. The eraser crumbs generated a soft gray dust along the road, and she blew them off, watching the sidewalk come back clean. Her first eraser was worn down to a stub, its erosion a badge of all the correcting she'd done today, and she dropped it in the tray and picked up a new one.

Mr. Ruiz wandered past, looked at the second sheet, and raised his eyebrows. "Now that's a street. Fix the first one and tape both up so people can see the difference."

Penelope was already redrawing lamppost number one, tall and confident at the front, then number two a little shorter, then a little shorter, a little closer, all the way back. Marcus peered at her page over her shoulder and said, "Okay, I'm stealing your entire system."

"Steal away," Penelope said, and drew the final lamppost as a stub no bigger than her thumbnail, right at the edge of forever.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
story:
The writing club met in the back corner of the library every Tuesday, and Landon had learned to dread Tuesdays. Mrs. Okafor had returned his short story with one line at the top: "The dialogue punctuation needs work, and the climax is missing. Revise." He had read the page four times and still couldn't see what was wrong. Every time a character spoke, he had done what seemed obvious. He wrote: "I'm not afraid of the dark," with a period, then "said Tasha" right after it. Periods ended sentences. That was the rule he'd known since first grade.

Across the table, Priya was marking drafts with a red pen, and Landon noticed she kept drawing the same shape next to certain lines. He leaned over. She had circled a period, the one sitting before "she said" in Marisol's story. Then she circled an identical one in the next paragraph. Landon's stomach tightened. She wasn't circling random things. She was finding a pattern, and he was pretty sure his story was full of the same pattern.

He flipped to his own draft and read the sentences aloud under his breath, testing one against another. "Get down from there." Then: "shouted the guard." He looked at Priya's marks again. In the line she had circled, she had written a tiny correction: a comma inside the quotation marks where the period used to be. When a dialogue tag followed the spoken words, the comma went inside the quotes instead of the period. He tried it on his own line. "Get down from there," shouted the guard. It looked strange, like a sentence wearing someone else's coat, but every corrected line in Priya's stack matched it exactly.

"Give me yours," Priya said when he slid his draft across the table. He watched her pen move, and every period before "she said" or "he whispered" got replaced. "You too?" Marisol asked, peering over. "Every single one." Priya shrugged. "Mine had eleven."

Fixing the punctuation, though, forced Landon to see the other problem. His story was about a boy under siege from a talking crow that wouldn't leave his window, and the crow was dormant for whole pages, doing nothing while the boy wandered around being sad. There was no moment where everything turned. He had been hiding from it, he realized, because he didn't know how to make it happen. He wrote a new scene fast, the boy finally shouting the one true thing the crow had been waiting to hear, and it ended with a comma inside the quotation marks, and then "said the boy," and it felt like a door opening.

"Read it out loud," Marisol said, so he did, and when he reached the climax even Priya set her pen down. Then the bell rang, and everyone packed up, and Landon looked at his old draft lying in the trash where he'd crumpled it ten minutes earlier. Three days of work, gone, and the new ending only half finished. He pulled the crumpled page out anyway and smoothed it on the table. "You can't save all of it," Priya said, shouldering her bag. "Watch me," said Landon.
